lesson.title: Pronouns as Case Anchors (The Him-Case)
lesson.subtitle: Why only masculine articles change in the accusative (der → den, er → ihn)

hook.title: The 'Him-Case' Secret
hook.content: Every beginner wonders: Why does German change 'der' to 'den', 'ein' to 'einen', and 'er' to 'ihn' for direct objects, while feminine ('die/eine') and neuter ('das/ein') stay completely unchanged? The answer lies in your own native tongue. English does this exact thing: we say 'He saw the dog', but 'The dog bit HIM' (never 'bit he'). We say 'who' for the subject, but 'WHOM' for the object. That nasal ending is the ancient Indo-European direct object marker!

footnotes.title: The Accusative Nasal Marker
footnotes.content: Proto-Indo-European marked the masculine accusative with *-m. In High German, an unstressed final -m shifted to -n (him ↔ ihn, whom ↔ wen).

pattern.title: The Masculine Accusative -N Rhyme
pattern.content: In Proto-Germanic, neuter and feminine nouns never marked accusative differently from nominative. Masculine singular is the lone survivor that raises a flag with the letter '-N' whenever it receives an action: der ➔ den, ein ➔ einen, kein ➔ keinen, mein ➔ meinen, and er ➔ ihn (the twin of English 'him'). Feminine and neuter nouns remain steadfastly identical (die bleibt die, das bleibt das). Once you recognize the 'Him-Case', you never mistake accusative articles again.

footnotes.title: M → N Nasal Alignment
footnotes.content: English preserved the ancient accusative nasal in him/them/whom; German shifted final unstressed m to n in ihn/den/wen.

pattern.trap_note: Your mind will offer: “der becomes den because masculine.” The rule is smaller and more useful: the masculine tail moves because *him* moved. Ask which pronoun would replace the noun and the ending follows. Feminine and neuter objects keep their article because English her and it never changed shape either.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the masculine direct object article for 'a coffee' (ein + accusative -en):
exercises.explanation: Indefinite root 'ein' + masculine accusative marker '-en' = einen.

exercises.prompt: Match the English objective pronouns with their German accusative twins:
exercises.explanation: English preserved the ancient accusative/dative in him/me/thee/us; German preserves ihn/mich/dich/uns.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'der Kaffee' change to 'den Kaffee' in 'Ich trinke den Kaffee', but 'das Wasser' stays 'das Wasser'?
options: Because coffee is a hot beverage
In Germanic, only masculine singular marks the direct object with the nasal -n (cognate with English 'him' and 'whom')
Because trinken only changes masculine verbs
Neuter nouns are completely immune to verbs
exercises.target_answer: In Germanic, only masculine singular marks the direct object with the nasal -n (cognate with English 'him' and 'whom')
exercises.meaning: Masculine exclusivity of the accusative shift
exercises.explanation: Neuter and feminine nouns collapsed nominative and accusative in ancient Indo-European. Only masculine retains the distinct nasal accusative ending (-n in German, -m in English him/whom).

exercises.prompt: Complete with the masculine accusative: 'Ich habe _____ Traum' (ein + masculine direct object ending):
exercises.meaning: Ich habe einen Traum = I have a dream
exercises.explanation: 'Traum' is masculine (der Traum). As the direct object of haben, it takes the accusative 'einen'.

exercises.idea: you're at a café table, people-watching: you're drinking a coffee and looking for him
cues: Coffee is masculine and acted-on: ein → einen — the Him-Case on the article
The pronoun follows the same law: er → ihn (suchen needs no preposition — the 'for' is baked in)
exercises.target_answer: Ich trinke einen Kaffee und suche ihn
exercises.meaning: I am drinking a coffee and looking for him
exercises.explanation: Two clauses, one subject — and the masculine accusative shows twice: einen Kaffee, ihn. Him-case everywhere.

summary.outcome: Use den or einen for a masculine direct object and ihn for 'him' as an object.

use_example.german: Ich trinke einen Kaffee und suche ihn.
use_example.english: I drink a coffee and look for it.

summary.takeaway: Only masculine singular changes in the accusative: der → den, ein → einen, and er → ihn (the 'Him-Case').
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the den / einen / ihn case gym — the him-case drilled with real objects: trinke einen Kaffee, suche ihn.

twist.prompt: Same mouth, different order: I drink a coffee becomes I drink THE tea. (Careful — still masculine, still acted-on.)
twist.explanation: Tee is masculine too, so the Him-Case holds: der → den. Only the masculine article bends — feminine and neuter objects would have refused to change.

die.etymology_derivation: th → d. Sounds identical to emphatic English "thee".

das.shift_rule: TH → D + T → S / SS / Z
das.etymology_derivation: Double shift: th → d and final t → s.

tisch.context_phrase: Der Teller steht auf dem Tisch.
tisch.context_translation: The plate stands on the table.
tisch.etymology_derivation: Latin discus → Old English disc (dish/desk) → Old High German tisc (tisch, with d → t).

tag.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and y → g.

wolke.context_translation: A cloud is in the sky.
wolke.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *wolkn — the English cognate is archaic welkin 'sky'. [wiktionary]

rücken.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hrugjaz — the twin of English ridge; also the Rück- of zurückkommen. [wiktionary]

schlüssel.context_phrase: Der Schlüssel ist auf dem Tisch.
schlüssel.context_translation: The key is on the table.
schlüssel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *slutil, kin to schließen (close) — cognate with English slot. [wiktionary]

schinken.context_phrase: Ich möchte Schinken und Käse, bitte.
schinken.context_translation: I would like ham and cheese, please.
schinken.etymology_derivation: Schinken — originally a shank or thigh, from Proto-Germanic *skinkō; cognate with English shank and dialectal skink, a shin of beef. [wiktionary]

feind.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *fijandz, the hating one, the exact twin of English fiend; both are the participle of the same hate verb. [wiktionary]

etwas.etymology_derivation: From Old High German eddeshwaz: edde- (probably the old word behind oder 'or') + hwaz 'what' — originally something like or-what, hence something. [wiktionary]

morgens.context_translation: In the mornings I drink coffee.
morgens.etymology_derivation: Morgen + adverbial -s, from an old adverbial genitive — the twin formation of the English adverb mornings. [wiktionary]

wachsen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *wahsan, a class 6 strong verb (wuchs, gewachsen); the page documents cognate English wax in its older become sense — the moon still waxes. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
